plot: Second person, daily-life format: you are a keeper on the Flannan Isles in 1900; ten chapters cover why take the job, where it is, landing, the lamp, the schedule, food, the sea, the ship that saw no light, Moore alone in the empty tower, and the last chapter is the unsolved mystery of three vanished keepers.

beats.say: December 15, 1900. A steamship sails from Philadelphia toward Scotland. In the dark, near a tiny island, the crew looks for the lighthouse beam. It isn't there.
Rule number one. The lamp never goes out. Not in a storm. Not when you're sick. Not ever. Understand?
Understood. But we're twenty miles from the nearest town. What could possibly go wrong?

Tonight, you're a lighthouse keeper on the Flannan Isles, in the winter of 1900. You'll learn the job, the rules, and the sea. And at the very end, a mystery that nobody has solved in over a hundred years.
Chapter one. Why would anyone take this job?
Be honest. Why would anybody choose to live on a rock in the ocean?
A steady paycheck, and a house to live in. Nobody bosses you around, as long as the light keeps shining.
In 1900, a steady paycheck was a big deal. Fishing and farming could leave a family with nothing after one bad season. Lighthouse work was safe, respected, and it came with a roof over your head.
And this lighthouse was brand new. It was first lit on December 7, 1899, just one year before our story. Its builders had spent four years getting it done.
Chapter two. Where on Earth are you?
Welcome to Eilean Mor. It's the biggest of the Flannan Isles. Sailors call them the Seven Hunters.
The island sits about twenty miles west of the Isle of Lewis, off the coast of Scotland. Past it, there's nothing but open Atlantic Ocean. Across that ocean is North America.
So if I look out the window, all I see is water?
All of it. Every day. You'll get used to it. Or you won't.
The cliffs here are about 148 feet tall. That's like a fourteen-story building. The builders had to haul every stone, every beam and every bag of cement up those cliffs, straight from small boats.
They even built a little railway to carry supplies uphill, pulled by a cable and a small steam engine. That's how much work it took to put one light on one rock.
Chapter three. How do you even get on the island?
I almost fell in the water when the boat came in. Is it always like that?
Always. You wait for the swell, you jump, and you pray the boatman times it right. Some days, no boat can land at all.
That matters. A supply ship came every few weeks, but only if the sea allowed it. A storm could keep a ship away for days. If you ran out of something, you went without.
Chapter four. The job itself. The light.
Come on up. This is what everything is for.

At the top of the tower sat an enormous glass lens, built like a beehive made of glass rings. It took the light from one small flame and bent it into a beam you could see from more than twenty miles away.

The lamp burned paraffin, a kind of lamp oil. The light used about twenty barrels of it in a year. Someone had to carry it up the tower, fill the lamp, and keep every piece of glass spotless, every single day.
The glass is already covered in salt. I just cleaned it yesterday!
Then clean it again. A dirty lens means a dim light. And a dim light means a ship on the rocks.
That's the point of the job. Out in the dark, a captain steering a ship sees your light, and knows exactly where the rocks are. If your light is dim, or dead, his life is in your hands.
Chapter five. Your day.

Four men shared the work. Three stayed on the rock at a time, while the fourth rested on shore. The men on the island were a principal keeper, an assistant keeper, and a third man. They called the third man the Occasional, because he filled in when somebody was away.
At night, one of us is always awake. We trade the watches so nobody gets worn out.
Every day, the keepers wrote down the weather and anything strange in the log. Quick notes went on a slate first, and later got copied into the book. Remember that slate. It comes back in a minute.
So it's lamp, glass, log, watch, and then again tomorrow?
That's the job. Do it right for years, and nobody will ever notice you.
And there's one rule above all the others. The light must never be left alone. If a keeper is missing, the others have to stay and keep it burning. Leaving the lamp unwatched was a serious offense.
Chapter six. What do you eat, and who do you talk to?
Please tell me dinner isn't more canned fish.
Canned food, salted meat, and bread, mostly. Be glad when the supply boat shows up with something fresh.
Think of a camping trip that lasts for weeks. The same food. The same three faces. And a wind that never quiets down, howling around the tower day and night.
The Northern Lighthouse Board picked its keepers carefully. These men had to be steady, careful, and able to live with two other people in a small house for weeks, with no one else to talk to.
Do you ever miss people? Home, I mean?
Every single day. But the sea is worse than the quiet. Come outside and I'll show you.
Chapter seven. The sea.

On this island, the danger isn't a ship hitting the rocks. It's the water itself. Down at the west landing, there's a box bolted into the rock to hold the ropes and tools for landing boats. That box sits about 108 feet above the sea. Ten stories up.
That's ten stories up! The water can't reach that high. Can it?
In the worst storms, it can. The sea comes up the cliff like a hand. Never stand near the edge.

Keepers took their gear seriously, because losing it cost money. One researcher found that keeper Thomas Marshall had once been fined five shillings, when a huge gale washed his equipment away. Keep that in mind. It matters later.
Chapter eight. Back to that steamship from Philadelphia.

The steamer was called the Archtor. It was sailing to a port in Scotland called Leith, and the weather was rough. On the night of December 15, the crew kept looking for the Flannan light. They never saw it.
The ship docked in Leith on December 18. Only then did the crew report that the lighthouse had been dark. That meant the lighthouse board didn't hear about it for three days.
A relief ship, the Hesperus, was supposed to bring supplies and a fresh keeper. But bad weather held it back, and it didn't reach the island until December 26. Eleven days after the light went dark.
When the Hesperus finally arrived, something was wrong right away. There was no flag flying on the flagpole. And the supply boxes the keepers normally left out for the ship weren't there.
Captain Jim Harvie blew the ship's whistle. He fired a flare. Nobody came down to the landing. Nobody waved. The island was silent.
Chapter nine. One man goes up to look.
I'm going up. Maybe they're sick. Maybe they can't hear us.
The relief keeper, Joseph Moore, was put ashore. He went up the steep path to the lighthouse completely alone.
He found the gate to the compound closed. He found the main door closed, too. He called out for the keepers. Nobody answered.
Hello? Ducat? Marshall? It's Moore! Hello?
Inside, the beds were unmade. The clock had stopped, because nobody had wound it. The three men were nowhere to be found.
But one thing made no sense. The lamps had been cleaned. They'd been refilled with oil. Everything was ready for the night. Someone had finished the job, and then simply left.
Moore found a set of oilskins, the heavy waterproof coat keepers wore in storms. It was hanging inside. That meant at least one man had gone out into rough weather without it.
I searched every room. Every corner. They aren't here. They aren't anywhere.

Captain Harvie sent a message back to the mainland. It said, quote, a dreadful accident has happened at the Flannans. The three keepers, Ducat, Marshall and the Occasional, have disappeared from the island.
Chapter ten. The last chapter. What really happened to the three keepers?
The search team checked the whole island. The east landing was fine. But the west landing told a different story.
That box, the one nearly ten stories above the sea, was smashed open. Rope and tools were thrown all over the rocks. Iron railings were bent over like soft wire.

The iron railway track beside the path had been ripped out of its concrete. A rock that weighed more than a ton, about as much as a small car, had been shoved out of place. And up on top of the cliff, over 200 feet above the water, chunks of grass had been torn away.
beats.text: A ROCK AS HEAVY AS A CAR

beats.say: On December 29, a lighthouse board superintendent named Robert Muirhead arrived to investigate. He had hired all three men himself. This wasn't just a job for him. It was personal.
I want to know what happened to my men. Nothing else matters.
Muirhead said some of the damage at the west landing was, quote, difficult to believe unless actually seen. And then he studied the clothes left behind in the lighthouse.
beats.text: SOME DAMAGE WAS HARD TO BELIEVE

beats.say: He decided that two of the keepers, Ducat and Marshall, had worn their oilskins and gone down to the west landing. The third man, Donald McArthur, had run out in his shirt sleeves. His coat was still hanging on its peg.

Muirhead's conclusion: after dinner on Saturday, December 15, the men went down to secure the rope box. An unusually huge wave rushed up the cliff, climbed above them, and came crashing down, sweeping all of them into the sea.
Just one wave? That's all it took?
Think about that fine. Marshall had been punished once for losing his gear in a gale. One researcher thinks he and Ducat may have gone down to save the equipment, to avoid being fined again.
And McArthur? Some people think he saw a huge wave coming and ran down to warn his friends. A man who left his post, and his coat, to save them. Then the sea took him too.

Scientists have studied the island. The west landing sits in a narrow gap in the cliffs, and it ends in a cave. When a big storm wave rushes into that gap, the water has nowhere to go but up, and it can explode out with terrifying force.

But a plain accident didn't make a good story. So over the years, wilder ones got added. People said a sea serpent had snatched them. They said spies had kidnapped them. They said the men ran away to start new lives. And some blamed a ghost ship called the Phantom of the Seven Hunters.
You may have read about a spooky log, where Marshall wrote about a terrible storm, Ducat being silent, and McArthur crying. Those pages were never real.

A researcher named Mike Dash looked into it for the magazine Fortean Times. He found that the scary diary was made up, added to the story long after. And no storms were reported in that area on the days it described.
In 1912, a poet named Wilfrid Gibson wrote a famous poem about the lighthouse. It describes an overturned chair and an uneaten meal on the table. None of that was real either. Moore never saw it.

So here's what we truly don't know. If it was just a wave, why were both doors closed? Who closed them? Why did one man leave his coat, but not the others? And did the three men really leave the lamp unwatched, knowing the rule?

No bodies were ever found. No note. No witness. Some experts think a fight on the cliff may have ended in tragedy. Others think rogue waves swept them off one at a time, as they tried to save each other.
After the accident, new keepers took over, and the lighthouse kept working for decades. It was finally made automatic in 1971, so no human has had to live there since.

So what really happened? Most historians say a giant wave. The doors, the coat and the missing log pages are the pieces that don't fit. And that's why people still talk about it more than a century later.
I think I'd still take the job. But I'd never go near that west landing in a storm.

So tell me honestly. Twenty miles from anywhere, canned food, endless wind, and a lamp that must never go out. Would you have taken the job? Tell me in the comments, and subscribe for more true history.

long.title: Your Job: Keep the Light On, 20 Miles From Land (1900) 🔦
long.description:
Would you have taken the job? Tell me in the comments.

In December 1900, three lighthouse keepers vanished from the Flannan Isles, 20 miles off Scotland. Here is what the job was really like: the giant glass lens, the canned food, the swell that can climb ten stories up a cliff, and what relief keeper Joseph Moore found when he walked in alone.
